title: Schools, Civilization, and The Odyssey
author: Sustainable Schools
summary: Writing at the start of a new school year, this Sustainable Schools piece uses Homer's Odyssey, and specifically the Greek concept of xenia, or guest-friendship, to argue that schools perform a quietly civilizing function that goes far beyond instruction. The author walks through Telemachus's welcome of a stranger and contrasts it with Paris's violation of the same hospitality code, which triggers the fall of Troy, to establish Homer's larger point: civilizations that abandon their own rules of mutual obligation collapse, even when the individual transgressors survive. Citing Matthew Yglesias's reading of the poem as an allegory of institutional unraveling, the piece positions teachers as the opposite of Homer's self-interested raiders, caretakers who keep faith with a shared social contract while other parts of society defect from it. The concrete image of a family showing up at a schoolhouse door on Monday and having a bus at their house by Tuesday is offered as proof that schools' hospitality is not rhetorical but structural and reliable. The essay closes by framing the return of the school year itself as a renewal of this intergenerational contract, arguing that a society's willingness to look out for the next generation is what makes it, in the ancient sense, civilized.
points: The author uses the Greek concept of xenia (guest-friendship) from The Odyssey as a lens for understanding why schools' unconditional welcome of every child is a civilizing, not merely bureaucratic, act.
Drawing on Matthew Yglesias's reading of the poem, the piece argues that Homer's 'heroes' are actually the undoers of Mycenaean civilization, having defected from shared rules for personal gain.
Teachers are cast as the structural opposite of Yglesias's 'disorganized raiders': stewards who keep an intergenerational social contract running while other institutions falter.
The requirement that schools admit every child regardless of circumstance is framed as a form of concrete hospitality with real infrastructure behind it, not an abstract ideal.

The piece closes by tying the start of a new school year to this civilizing function: schools sustain collective prosperity precisely because they still practice reciprocal care as a matter of course.
quotes: Telemachus is following the rules of xenia, an ancient Greek concept of hospitality or, as it is sometimes translated, "guest-friendship". There are rules about what should be offered (food and wine) and when business should be discussed (after the food and wine) and who should receive the hospitality (strangers, foreigners, the poor, and anyone else who properly asks for it).

Homer repeatedly contrasts characters who do their duty with those who don't. The consequences do not always fall to the shirkers themselves, but they are often felt by the people around them as tragedy swallows their friends and family.

It is the basis of civilized life, actually, to treat strangers with kindness and follow rules that may inconvenience the individual for the betterment of all. It is no accident, after all, that polite rule-followers may be described as civil, and a collection of polite rule-followers may be called a civilization.
Teachers are the opposite of the "disorganized raiders" Yglesias criticizes for their role in societal decline. Teachers are caretakers at home, keeping the kingdom while everyone else is out to sea.

A family can show up at the schoolhouse door on Monday, and by Tuesday the bus will come to their house to pick up their child. The yellow school bus is not quite a limousine, but it's not far off from that level of service.
When teachers care for other people's children, they set in motion an inter-generational social contract and remind us that we are more prosperous when we look out for each other.
